title: Tankora Powder
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: Half a cup of powdered peanuts from kulikuli with a quarter cup of toasted corn flour — the de-oiled peanut is what makes it a powder rather than a paste.
longDesc: Tankora is the dry coating for chichinga and the reason it works is the kulikuli: peanuts that have had their oil pressed out, so the powder stays dry instead of clumping into butter. Half a cup of that powder goes with a quarter cup of toasted corn flour, made from a quarter cup of toasted ground white popcorn, plus dried ground red pepper, dried ginger and salt to taste. Optional additions are dried powdered green bell pepper, mace and ground white pepper. The instruction is one line: mix all of the ingredients together.
ingredients: 1/4 cup toasted corn flour — from 1/4 cup toasted, ground white popcorn
Dried ground red pepper, to taste — about 1/4-1/2 tsp
Dried ground ginger, to taste — about 1/2 tsp
Salt, to taste — maybe 1/4 tsp if the peanuts are salted
1/2 tsp dried powdered green bell pepper
steps: Press the oil from roasted peanuts to make kulikuli, then powder it (GHA072).
Toast a quarter cup of white popcorn and grind it to a flour.
Combine the peanut powder and the toasted corn flour.
Add the dried red pepper, dried ginger and salt to taste.
Add any of the optional green bell pepper powder, mace or white pepper.
Mix all of the ingredients together.
chefTips: The peanuts must be de-oiled. Ordinary ground peanuts turn to butter under pressure and will clump — kulikuli, with the oil pressed out, stays a dry powder.
Toasted ground white popcorn is her corn flour, which is an unusual and clever route to it. Toasting is what gives the nutty depth.
Salt only if the peanuts were unsalted. Her note is about a quarter teaspoon if they were salted — taste first.
Mace is an unusual inclusion and it is optional. It gives a warm, faintly floral note under the pepper.
Others use seasoning cubes in place of some of the salt and savoury depth, by her own note. That is what the elaborate chef version at GHA062 does, with ten of them.
Keep it dry and sealed. Any moisture and the peanut powder cakes.
Equal parts by feel is roughly two of peanut powder to one of corn flour, which is the backbone of the blend.
commonMistakes: Using ordinary ground peanuts rather than de-oiled kulikuli.
Grinding the corn so fine it becomes starch rather than flour.
sources: Adapted from 'Recipes #39 and 40: Kuli kuli and tankora', betumiblog.blogspot.com, Wednesday 3 February 2010. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Posted by Fran at 4:43 PM'. Quantities confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS).

Ingredients exactly as printed: 1/2 cup powdered peanuts from kulikuli; 1/4 cup toasted corn flour (from 1/4 cup toasted, ground white popcorn); dried ground red pepper to taste (~1/4-1/2 teaspoon); dried ground ginger to taste (~1/2 teaspoon); salt to taste (maybe 1/4 teaspoon if peanuts salted); optional 1/2 teaspoon dried powdered green bell pepper, 1/4 teaspoon mace, 1/2 teaspoon ground white pepper.
METHOD, verbatim and complete: 'Mix all of the ingredients together.' That is the entire method as printed.
SINGLE-PASS note: 'others use seasoning cubes'. That is corroborated by the chef version at GHA062, whose suya blend contains ten of them.

THE KULIKULI DEPENDENCY is what makes this blend work and it is published at GHA072 from the same post. Peanuts with the oil pressed out behave entirely differently from whole ground peanuts, and the source treats the two as separate ingredients.

TOASTED GROUND WHITE POPCORN as the route to toasted corn flour is documented nowhere else in this collection. The more usual product is ablemanu, the toasted corn flour that binds ayikple (GHA046) and aprapransa (GHA010).
NO YIELD is printed. The twelve servings above is an editorial reading of three quarters of a cup of blend used at half a cup per three-serving batch of chichinga.

ON THE NAMES: tankora in Ghana, yaji in northern Nigeria, and 'suya spice' in diaspora usage. The blends are closely related but not identical — the Ghanaian version leans on de-oiled peanut and toasted corn, while the documented chef version (GHA062) uses peanut butter powder and no corn at all.
storage: Months in a sealed jar kept dry.
healthBenefits: De-oiled peanut powder is high in protein with much of the fat removed.
Toasted maize adds fibre and B vitamins.
Ginger and pepper both carry documented bioactive compounds.
culturalNote: Tankora is sold in little newspaper twists beside the chichinga grill so you can dust on more as you eat, and the de-oiled peanut at its heart is a genuinely clever piece of food technology — a way to get peanut flavour as a dry powder centuries before anyone sold defatted peanut flour in a packet.
